lessons.title: Interest Rate Cycles: RBI, Bond Yields, and Equity Valuations

body.text: Interest rates are the price of time, and every asset is a claim on future money. When rates rise, future money is worth less today, so bonds, shares and property all get repriced. The assets whose payoff lies furthest in the future move the most.

children.text: Lesson 1.3 introduced credit as the engine of cycles and showed the RBI's repo rate at its turning points. Lesson 4.1 showed how oil feeds inflation, which pushes the RBI to act. This lesson follows the chain to the end: how a repo rate decision travels through the bond market to your home loan, why bond prices move opposite to yields, how rates change what investors will pay for shares, and why the stock market so often seems to react to rate changes in the "wrong" direction.
From Mint Street to Your EMI

children.text: Since October 2019, banks have had to link new floating-rate retail and small business loans to an external benchmark, which for most banks is the repo rate. That means the rate cycle now reaches household budgets far faster than before. Between May 2022 and February 2023 the RBI raised the repo rate from 4% to 6.5%. Here is what a rate cycle of that size can do to a typical home loan.

body.label: ₹50 lakh home loan over 20 years
body.value: EMI of about ₹38,000 at 6.75% vs about ₹45,800 at 9.25%
body.context: A 2.5 percentage point rise in the loan rate adds about ₹7,775 a month, roughly ₹18.7 lakh extra over 20 years if the rate stayed there. In practice many banks extend the loan tenure rather than raise the EMI, which shifts the cost into later years.

children.text: Bond Yields: The Market's Verdict on Rates

markDefs.definition: The annual return an investor earns by buying a bond at its current market price and holding it to maturity. When the price falls, the yield rises, and when the price rises, the yield falls.

children.text: The RBI sets only the shortest rate. Everything longer is set by the bond market, and the most watched number in India is the

on the 10-year government bond, often called the 10-year G-sec. It reflects where investors expect the repo rate to be over the coming decade, what they expect inflation to do, how much the government is borrowing, and how much foreign money is flowing in. It is the benchmark against which almost every other long-term investment in India, including shares, gets judged.

body.title: India 10-year government bond yield at major turning points (approximate)

children.text: Match the peaks and troughs to earlier lessons: the 2008 oil and inflation spike, the emergency cuts after Lehman, the 2013 taper tantrum, the IL&FS stress of 2018, the COVID rate cuts and the 2022 global inflation shock. Every major market episode in Chapter 3 shows up here too. In June 2024, Indian government bonds were also added to JP Morgan's widely tracked emerging market bond index, a structural change expected to bring steadier foreign demand for Indian debt.
Why Bond Prices Fall When Yields Rise

Suppose you own a 10-year bond with a face value of ₹100 paying a fixed coupon of ₹7 a year, bought when market yields were 7%. If the RBI hikes and new 10-year bonds now pay 8%, nobody will pay you ₹100 for a bond paying only ₹7. The price of your bond has to fall until its yield matches the market. The price is simply the present value of all the future payments, discounted at the current yield.

body.caption: C = annual coupon, F = face value, y = current market yield, n = years to maturity
A 10-year, 7% coupon bond with ₹100 face value at different market yields

body.title: Price the Bond
body.prompt: Using the formula above, what is the price of the 10-year, ₹7 coupon, ₹100 face value bond if the market yield rises to 8%? Round to two decimal places.
body.explanation: The ten ₹7 coupons discounted at 8% are worth about ₹46.97, and the ₹100 repaid in year 10 is worth 100 ÷ 1.08 to the power 10, about ₹46.32. Total ≈ ₹93.29, a fall of about 6.7%. Notice the asymmetry: a 1 point cut in yield raises the price by about 7.4%, while a 1 point rise lowers it by about 6.7%. A quick rule of thumb uses the bond's modified duration, about 7 for this bond: price change ≈ −7 × change in yield.

body.text: Debt mutual funds are not immune to rate cycles. Funds holding long-term government bonds, such as gilt and long-duration funds, gain when yields fall and lose when they rise. Many investors who bought these funds after strong returns in a rate-cutting phase were surprised by losses when the cycle turned, as in mid 2013 when the RBI tightened sharply to defend the rupee, and again in 2022. "Safe from default" is not the same as "safe from price swings".

body.title: Quick Check
body.textWithBlank: When market interest rates and bond yields rise, the prices of existing bonds ___.
body.explanation: An existing bond's coupon is fixed, so when new bonds pay more, the old bond's price must fall until its yield matches the market. The longer the bond's maturity, the bigger the price move for the same change in yield.

children.text: A share is like a bond with no fixed coupon and no maturity: a claim on all the company's future profits. The same discounting logic applies, but more strongly, because much of a company's value lies in profits many years away. The rate investors use to discount those profits is the risk-free government bond yield plus an extra return for taking equity risk. When bond yields rise, that discount rate rises, and the fair P/E falls. Companies whose profits are expected mostly in the distant future, fast-growing companies, feel it the most.

body.title: Show me the math: why growth stocks are more rate-sensitive

children.text: A simple valuation model for a company that pays out part of its earnings and grows steadily gives a forward P/E of:

content.caption: r = required return (bond yield plus equity risk premium), g = long-term earnings growth. Only valid when g is below r.
What a 1 percentage point rise in required return does to two hypothetical companies

children.text: The same one point rise in rates cut the growth company's fair P/E by a third, more than twice the hit to the steady company, because the gap between r and g was so narrow. Real models are more complex, but the direction holds. It is why the most expensive growth stocks and new-age tech listings fell hardest when global rates rose in 2022.

body.title: Test Yourself
body.question: Global bond yields rise sharply over six months. Which kind of Indian listed company would you expect to see the biggest fall in its P/E multiple, all else equal?
options: A mature, cash-rich company paying out most of its profits as dividends with low growth
A loss-making or low-profit company whose valuation depends on large profits expected ten years from now
A company with no debt and stable profits growing in line with inflation
All companies' P/E multiples fall by exactly the same percentage
body.explanation: The further in the future a company's expected profits lie, the more a higher discount rate shrinks their present value. A company valued on distant future profits behaves like a very long-duration bond, so it is the most sensitive to rising yields. This is why many new-age technology stocks fell far more than steady consumer or utility companies in 2022.

children.text: Why Markets Seem to React the Wrong Way

If higher rates are bad for shares and lower rates are good, why did the Nifty crash while the RBI was cutting in early 2020, and end 2022 higher while the RBI was hiking? Because markets care about why rates are moving and what comes next, and they move ahead of the decisions. Rate cuts often arrive because growth is collapsing. Rate hikes often arrive because demand is strong. What matters most is the direction of inflation and real rates, and whether the policy change is already priced in.

Real estate developers, as home loans get cheaper

body.text: US interest rates matter to Indian markets too. When the US Federal Reserve raised its policy rate from near zero to above 5% between March 2022 and July 2023, the gap between Indian and US yields narrowed. Foreign investors had less reason to hold Indian assets, which contributed to heavy foreign selling in 2022 and pressure on the rupee. Watch the Fed as well as the RBI.

body.title: Reading an RBI Policy Like a Cycle-Aware Investor
steps: Note what the RBI did to the repo rate, and whether markets expected it
Check the policy stance: is the RBI signalling more cuts, more hikes or a pause?
Read the inflation and growth projections, since they hint at the next moves
Watch the 10-year G-sec yield in the days after the policy, which shows how the bond market read it
Ask why rates are moving: a crisis, weak growth, falling inflation, or overheating
Consider which of your holdings are rate-sensitive, including debt funds, and whether your floating-rate loans will reset

body.title: "The RBI Is Cutting, Buy Everything"
body.scenario: The RBI has cut the repo rate twice in three months and signalled more cuts. A colleague in Gurugram has read that rate-cut cycles are good for shares. He plans to move his entire emergency fund from a liquid fund into a long-duration gilt fund, and his equity SIPs into a real estate sector fund and small cap NBFC stocks, "to ride the rate cycle".
body.prompt: Using this lesson, what should he think about before acting?
body.modelAnswer: His basic logic has some truth: falling rates do tend to help bond prices, real estate, NBFCs and growth stocks. But several things are missing. First, why is the RBI cutting? If cuts are driven by falling inflation with stable growth, as in 2015 to 2017, rate-sensitive assets often do well. If they respond to a slowdown or a credit accident, as in 2008 or 2020, shares can keep falling after the cuts begin. Second, markets move ahead of decisions: by the time two cuts have happened and more are signalled, bond yields and rate-sensitive stocks may already have priced in much of the benefit. Third, cycles turn. A long-duration gilt fund can lose money if inflation surprises and yields rise, as in 2013 and 2022, so it is the wrong home for an emergency fund, which needs stability and quick access. Fourth, NBFCs and real estate are exposed to the credit cycle as well as rates, as IL&FS showed in 2018. A cycle-aware approach would keep the emergency fund liquid and stable, keep equity SIPs diversified, and if he wants to tilt toward beneficiaries of lower rates, do it modestly and based on an understanding of why rates are falling.

children.text: Rate cycles and commodity cycles do not lift or sink every stock equally. They change which sectors lead the market. Lesson 4.3 traces that rotation across India's market eras, from the infrastructure darlings of 2007 to the consumer staples of the grind years and the PSU and capital goods rally of the 2020s.

body.text: Yields, rates and loan examples in this lesson are approximate and for illustration, and figures after mid 2025 are not covered. The bond and valuation tables are simplified models, not forecasts. Actual EMIs depend on your lender's terms. Nothing here is a recommendation to buy or sell any security or fund, or investment advice.
